doc.charts_a11y_desc: All charts include screen-reader accessible data tables and follow WAI-ARIA standards for focus management in interactive legends.
doc.charts_anatomy_axis: Labels and scales (X/Y) that provide context for the data values.
doc.charts_anatomy_chart: The main visualization area containing bars, lines, segments, or points.
doc.charts_anatomy_tooltip: Displays specific values when the user hovers over a data point.
doc.charts_areachart_desc: Similar to LineChart but emphasizes the magnitude of change.
doc.charts_barchart_desc: Best for comparing quantities across categories.
doc.charts_best_practice_1: Ensure high color contrast between data series for better visibility, especially in dark mode.
doc.charts_choice_matrix_desc: Select the appropriate chart type based on the relationship you want to highlight (comparison, trend, part-to-whole, etc.).
doc.charts_components_desc: This collection includes various charting components for data visualization:
doc.charts_desc: Visual representation of data with various chart types
doc.calendarHeatmap_desc: GitHub-style activity graph for visualizing continuity
doc.calendarHeatmap_long_desc: A component for visualizing activity levels or data density over time in a calendar grid format, similar to the GitHub contribution graph.
doc.calendarHeatmap_design_intent: CalendarHeatmap is designed to provide a high-level overview of activity patterns and consistency over time. By using color intensity to represent data density, it helps users quickly identify streaks, trends, and gaps in their activity history.
doc.calendarHeatmap_anatomy_cell: An individual square representing a single day. Its color indicates the activity level.
doc.calendarHeatmap_anatomy_legend: A key explaining the relationship between colors and activity levels.
doc.calendarHeatmap_anatomy_label: Day and month labels providing temporal context.
doc.calendarHeatmap_content_guidelines: Ensure the color scale has sufficient contrast between levels. Use tooltips to provide the exact date and count for each cell.
doc.calendarHeatmap_a11y_spec: Each cell should have an aria-label or title indicating the date and value. Tooltips provide accessible information on focus and hover.
doc.calendarHeatmap_keyboard_desc: Users can navigate through activity cells using Tab. Focused cells display a tooltip with details.
doc.calendarHeatmap_scenario_github: Activity Tracking: Visualizing coding contributions or exercise streaks over the past year.
doc.calendarHeatmap_scenario_density: Data Density: Representing system load or error rates across different days of the week.
doc.charts_design_intent: Charts provide visual representations of complex datasets to help users identify patterns, trends, and outliers at a glance. They aim to make data understandable through clear, accessible, and theme-compliant visualizations.
doc.charts_funnelchart_desc: Shows the progression of data through a process.
doc.charts_gauge_desc: Visualizes a single value within a range (e.g., progress toward goal).
doc.charts_heatmap_desc: Represents data density or values through color variations.
doc.charts_keyboard_desc: Use Tab to focus on interactive chart elements. Left/Right arrows navigate through data points or legend items.
doc.charts_props_desc: Core props such as data, height, width, title, and animated are shared across all chart components. The table above shows AreaChart as a representative example; see each chart's type definition for chart-specific props.
doc.charts_linechart_desc: Ideal for showing trends over time.
doc.charts_piechart_desc: Shows parts of a whole proportionally.
doc.charts_radarchart_desc: Compares multiple quantitative variables across three or more dimensions.
doc.charts_recharts_note: Each chart is built using Recharts for high performance and accessibility.
doc.charts_scatterchart_desc: Visualizes relationships between two numerical variables.
doc.charts_scenario_dashboard: Monitoring system performance metrics or business KPIs in real-time.
doc.charts_scenario_report_desc: Visualizing monthly trends in sales, user growth, or resource consumption.
doc.charts_treemap_desc: Displays hierarchical data using nested rectangles.
doc.chatui_a11y_2: Send button can be triggered with Enter key
doc.chatui_a11y_desc: The composer sends on Enter and inserts a newline on Shift+Enter, which is the convention people expect from a chat box but is not something a screen reader can discover, so state it in the surrounding copy if the surface is unfamiliar. The icon-only controls for attaching a file and sending take their names from the translations rather than from the glyph. Message bubbles are plain content: give the transcript region a name and, when messages arrive without the user acting, announce them through a live region you control.

doc.chatui_anatomy_root: The outermost container managing state and layout.
doc.chatui_best_practice_1: Use ChatUI consistently across your application to maintain a predictable user experience.
doc.chatui_best_practice_2: Test ChatUI behavior across different screen sizes and input methods to ensure accessibility.
doc.chatui_bp_a11y_desc: To ensure screen reader compatibility, assign appropriate ARIA roles to the message list and notify new messages using aria-live.
doc.chatui_bp_autoscroll_desc: Implement auto-scroll to newest messages for better UX
doc.chatui_bp_avatars_desc: Display avatars for multi-user conversations to help identify senders
doc.chatui_bp_loading_desc: Show typing indicators or loading states when appropriate
doc.chatui_bp_position_desc: Use `position="left"` for received messages and `position="right"` for sent messages
doc.chatui_c_avatar: Avatar component with image support and fallback text
doc.chatui_c_input: Input field with send button for composing messages

doc.chatui_f_avatar_desc: Display user avatars with images or fallback text
doc.chatui_f_input_desc: Send messages with button click or Enter key
doc.chatui_f_variants_desc: Different styles for system, admin, or bot messages
doc.chatui_interactive_desc: A fully functional chat with message sending and auto-scroll:
doc.chatui_keyboard_desc: Message list can be navigated and focused using standard keyboard shortcuts. Input field supports sending messages with Enter.

doc.chatui_scenario_1: Customer Support: Real-time assistance for users navigating complex workflows.
doc.chatui_scenario_2: Internal Team Comms: A lightweight collaboration tool within a project management dashboard.

doc.sortable_list_long_desc: A component that allows users to reorder list items via drag and drop, providing a smooth and accessible way to manage prioritized or ordered data.
doc.sortable_list_design_intent: SortableList is designed to provide an intuitive interface for tasks that require manual ordering, such as task prioritization, menu management, or photo galleries. It combines the simplicity of a standard list with the interactivity of drag-and-drop, ensuring accessibility through full keyboard support.
doc.sortable_list_choice_matrix_desc: Choose based on the complexity and dimensionality of the data being reordered.
doc.sortable_list_choice_self_when: When you need to reorder a single vertical or horizontal list of items.
doc.sortable_list_choice_kanban_when: When items need to be moved across multiple columns or categories (2D reordering).
doc.sortable_list_anatomy_root: The outer container that manages the drag-and-drop context and drop zones.
doc.sortable_list_anatomy_item: Individual draggable element. Can contain any content.
doc.sortable_list_anatomy_handle: Optional dedicated area used to initiate the drag operation. Recommended for complex items to prevent accidental drags.
doc.sortable_list_a11y_desc: Fully supports WAI-ARIA standards. Items are navigable via Tab, and reordering can be performed using Arrow keys when an item is focused.
doc.sortable_list_scenario_1: Task Management: Prioritizing a 'To-Do' list by dragging the most important tasks to the top.
doc.sortable_list_scenario_2: Menu Editor: Reordering navigation links for a website footer or sidebar.
doc.sortable_list_best_practice_1: Always provide visual feedback (like a placeholder or line) to indicate where the item will be dropped.
doc.sortable_list_best_practice_2: Ensure that the drag-and-drop action is not the only way to perform the reordering; keyboard support is essential for accessibility.
doc.sortable_list_keyboard_desc: Tab to focus an item. Use Arrow Up/Down (or Left/Right) to move the item in the list. Focus indicators clearly show the active item.

doc.stats_a11y_desc: The trend arrow is aria-hidden, because it repeats visually what the delta text already says. That means the direction has to be present in the text itself: a value of "12%" with only an upward arrow is announced as "12%" with no indication of which way it moved. Write the change into the label or the value, and remember that the trend colour is likewise unavailable to a screen reader.

doc.virtuallist_best_practice_4: VirtualList and InfiniteScroll solve different problems and work well together — use InfiniteScroll to fetch data incrementally and VirtualList to keep rendering lightweight as items accumulate.

doc.virtuallist_choice_alt_table_when: When items need to be displayed in a tabular format with column headers and sorting.
doc.virtuallist_choice_self_when: When rendering large datasets (hundreds to tens of thousands of items) where full DOM rendering would degrade performance.
doc.virtuallist_custom_height_desc: Set itemHeight to match the actual height of your item content.
doc.virtuallist_desc: Efficiently renders large lists by virtualizing off-screen items
doc.virtuallist_design_intent: VirtualList provides a performant rendering strategy for large datasets by only mounting items currently visible in the viewport. This dramatically reduces DOM size and memory usage compared to rendering all items at once.
doc.virtuallist_keyboard_desc: Arrow keys navigate between list items. Tab moves focus to each interactive item. Enter or Space activates the focused item.
doc.virtuallist_large_dataset_desc: Even with 10,000 items, only a small subset is rendered in the DOM at any time.
doc.virtuallist_long_desc: A virtualized list component that efficiently handles large datasets by rendering only visible items.
doc.virtuallist_overscan_desc: The overscan prop controls how many extra items are rendered outside the visible area to reduce flickering during fast scrolling.

doc.virtuallist_scenario_2: Product Catalogs: Rendering extensive e-commerce listings while maintaining smooth scrolling performance.
doc.charts_color_desc: Pick the color by the job it does, not by the order the data happens to arrive in. A hue that means nothing invites the reader to ask what it means.
doc.charts_color_job_identity_desc: Telling series apart. Assign the five chart hues in fixed order so a series keeps its color when a filter removes its neighbours. Used by LineChart, AreaChart, BarChart, RadarChart, ScatterChart and PieChart — marks whose only route back to the legend is color.
doc.charts_color_job_magnitude_desc: One hue, light to dark. Used by Treemap, Heatmap, FunnelChart and CalendarHeatmap — shapes that already carry the value in their area or length, and that name themselves on the mark. Cycling hues there makes one shrinking quantity look like several different things.
doc.charts_color_job_state_desc: success, warning and danger are reserved for state. Never reuse them as a fourth series, and always pair them with a label — color alone is not a message.
doc.charts_color_area_note: The five chart hues are picked for thin marks — a 2px line, an 8px dot. Against the light surface all five clear 3:1; against the dark surface only chart-primary and chart-warning do, and the other three lean on the legend and the direct label instead. The numbers are in the table below. Large fills need the opposite: a treemap tile or a stacked band at that chroma shouts, and two saturated hues meeting along a long edge make the boundary vibrate. Tint them toward the surface instead, and let normal text ink sit on top.
doc.charts_color_gap_note: Where two fills touch — stacked bars, pie wedges, treemap tiles — leave a 2px gap in the surface color. The separation is what the eye reads as an edge; without it, adjacent colors blend into a third.
doc.charts_color_override_note: The chart hues are tokens, so you can swap them for your own. Two conditions have to survive the swap, and npm run check:chart-palette fails without them: neighbouring series stay apart for normal and for colorblind vision, and the state colors are not pulled in as extra series. Contrast against the surface is measured rather than enforced — aim for 3:1, and where a hue cannot reach it (at this chroma, blue on the dark surface cannot) keep the legend and the direct label that identify the series without color.
doc.charts_color_limit_note: Five series is the ceiling, and a sixth is not a sixth hue. Fold the tail into a single "Other", split into small multiples, or add a second encoding such as shape or texture. Generated hues drift into each other and stop being distinguishable long before they run out.
doc.charts_color_not_alone_note: Never let color be the only difference. Every chart that tells series apart by hue renders a legend, and it cannot be turned off — check:chart-palette fails if one is removed or made conditional. Charts that carry the value in area or length (Treemap, FunnelChart, Heatmap, GanttChart) name themselves on the mark instead. Contrast against the surface is measured, not enforced, so the legend is what keeps the chart readable with the color removed — for colorblind readers, in print, and under forced-colors mode.
doc.charts_color_evidence_desc: These numbers are not written here. They are produced by npm run check:chart-palette, the same guard that decides whether the palette ships, so re-picking a hue moves this table in the same commit. Light and dark are chosen separately: the same token is a different step and a different number in each.
doc.charts_color_evidence_col_light: Light — PCCS step, hex, contrast on surface
doc.charts_color_evidence_col_dark: Dark — PCCS step, hex, contrast on surface
doc.charts_color_evidence_row_surface: Surface the contrast is measured against

doc.jsondiff_intro: JsonDiffViewer compares two JSON values side-by-side or in unified form, with line-level diff highlighting. It serializes both values with JSON.stringify and delegates rendering to CodeDiffViewer.
doc.jsondiff_design_intent: Optimized for comparing API responses, webhook payloads, and configuration objects. By delegating to CodeDiffViewer with language=json, it inherits all diff controls while keeping its own API minimal.
doc.jsondiff_choice_self: Compare two JSON objects or arrays
doc.jsondiff_choice_jsonviewer: Display a single JSON value (no diff needed)
doc.jsondiff_a11y_1: Inherits all accessibility attributes from CodeDiffViewer.
doc.jsondiff_a11y_2: Apply and Reject buttons expose intent via visible label text.
doc.jsondiff_kb_tab: Move focus between Apply, Reject, Copy, and view-toggle buttons.
doc.jsondiff_content_guidelines_1: JsonDiffViewer serializes values with `JSON.stringify(value, null, indent)`. The default `indent` of 2 produces readable diffs; use 0 for compact comparisons.
doc.jsondiff_content_guidelines_2: Pass objects that share the same logical schema to produce meaningful line-level diffs.
doc.jsondiff_motion_desc: Inherits the static diff rendering of CodeDiffViewer. No animations.
doc.jsondiff_scenario_1_desc: Compare the before/after JSON payloads of a webhook or REST call to audit field-level changes.
doc.jsondiff_scenario_2_desc: Show a configuration object before and after an AI agent modifies it.
doc.jsondiff_practice_1: Pre-sort object keys before passing to keep diffs stable across serialization order changes.
doc.jsondiff_practice_2: Avoid passing deeply nested objects with large arrays — consider flattening or paginating for readability.
doc.jsondiff_responsive: Inherits CodeDiffViewer's responsive behavior: auto-switches to unified view below 640 px.
doc.jsondiff_i18n_desc: All user-facing labels inherit from CodeDiffViewer. Pass `filename` or `language` for context rather than embedding translated text in the value.
